metaDescription: See the banana prompt examples behind the viral Nano Banana edits, copy the exact line, add your own photo, and run the whole thing free in the Gemini app.
bodyHtml:
A banana prompt is the single line of text you hand to Google's Gemini image model, the one almost everyone now calls Nano Banana, to turn a plain photo into something worth posting. The official name is Gemini 2.5 Flash Image, and there is a sharper newer version, Nano Banana Pro, that arrived alongside Gemini 3 in late 2025. Most people landing here are not hunting for a folder of options. They want the one prompt they saw go around, the exact wording behind that action-figure shot or that storefront photo, so they can paste it, drop in their own face, and get the same thing. The grid above holds those exact lines, ready to copy.

Why one banana prompt can spread so far

The reason a single prompt catches on is that it produces a result that looks personal and slightly impossible at the same time. You see a friend posed as a boxed collectible figure, or standing in front of a shop with their own name on it, and the first thing you think is how. Then someone drops the wording in the comments, and within a day a few thousand people have run the same line with their own photo. That is the whole loop. The prompt travels, not the picture.

What makes Nano Banana suited to this is that it holds a face across a big change of scene. Older tools would give you a great background and a stranger's head. This model keeps the person recognizable while swapping almost everything else, so the same prompt works for you, for me, for anyone who pastes it. That consistency is the quiet reason these single prompts go around instead of dying after one lucky run.

The single banana prompts people actually copied

From what has been getting passed around since the model launched, a handful of banana prompts did most of the traveling. They are worth knowing because they show what the model is genuinely good at.

  • The action figure. You as a boxed collectible, plastic sheen, a little accessory beside you, often with fake packaging text. This one went the furthest because it reads instantly and almost always works.
  • The storefront. A photo of you standing outside a shop that carries your own name on the sign, lit like a real street.
  • The era swap. The same face moved into a 1970s film frame, or a 90s point-and-shoot snapshot, grain and faded color included.
  • The studio headshot. A casual selfie turned into a clean profile picture with soft key light and a plain backdrop.
  • The scene drop. You placed somewhere unlikely but believable, the kind of shot that made one popular tutorial describe sailing down a chocolate river.

Each of these is one prompt. You do not chain five edits together. You write a single clear line, give it a photo, and let it run.

Which model runs your banana prompt, standard or Pro

If your banana prompt feels weaker than the examples you saw, you might be on a different model than the person who posted it. The original, Gemini 2.5 Flash Image, is fast and cheap and fine for most edits. Nano Banana Pro is the heavier model that came with Gemini 3. It reasons more about what you asked, it knows more about the real world, and it is much better at one thing the first model fumbled: putting legible text into an image. If your prompt needs a readable sign, a label, a poster, or a name on a box, Pro is the one you want. For a quick face-keeping edit, the standard model is plenty.

Tip: if a prompt that asks for any words in the picture keeps coming back with garbled lettering, that is your sign to switch to Nano Banana Pro rather than rewrite the prompt.

Where you can run a banana prompt

The same line of text works in a few different places, and the cost and feel are not identical. Here is the short version.

WhereWhat it costsBest for
Gemini appFree tier, limits on heavy useCasual edits and trying a prompt the first time
Photoshop generativePaid, inside a Photoshop planEditors who want the result on a layer to refine
Gemini APIA few cents per imageBatches, apps, generating many at once
Third-party appsVaries, often creditsPeople who want presets and no setup

For almost everyone starting out, the Gemini app free tier is the answer. Run your banana prompt there, see if you like it, and only think about Photoshop or the API once you know the wording works. Nano Banana also showed up officially inside Photoshop in late 2025, so if you already live in that program you can edit on a layer instead of bouncing to a separate app.

Writing your own banana prompt from scratch

You do not have to wait for a viral one. A good single prompt follows a simple order, and you can build it in about a minute.

  1. Name the subject in a few words. A photo of me, the two of us, my dog.
  2. Say what must not change. Keep my exact face and skin tone is the line that saves most edits.
  3. Describe the one look you want. A boxed toy figure, a 90s film photo, a magazine headshot. One look, not three.
  4. Set the scene and the light. On a desk under soft light, outside at dusk, plain grey wall.
  5. Add any text last, and only if you need it. A small label that reads your name, switched to Pro if it has to be readable.

Glue those into one sentence and you have a working banana prompt. The discipline is keeping it to a single idea. The moment you ask for a new outfit and a new background and a new mood in the same line, the model starts dropping pieces.

When a banana prompt does not work

Most misses come from one of three things, and each has a fast fix.

The face came back wrong

Your look words are louder than your keep words. Move keep my exact face to the very front of the prompt and tone down the style language. Start from a sharp, well-lit photo too, because a soft input gives a soft, drifting face every time.

The text in the image is gibberish

This is the standard model's weak spot. Run the same prompt in Nano Banana Pro instead of fiddling with the wording. If you are stuck on the free model, keep the text very short, one or two words, and accept it may still wobble.

It refused outright

Nano Banana moderates hard. Photos of real people you did not take, anything with a public figure, and images of children get declined often, and it tends to say no upfront rather than generate and then block. If a prompt gets refused, change the subject or use a photo you clearly have the right to edit.

Pick one prompt from the grid, give it a clear photo, and run it three times before you decide. If you need words in the picture, switch to Pro. Keep the wording that lands, change one detail at a time after that, and a single banana prompt turns into a look you can repeat whenever you want.

faqs.a: It is one line of text you paste into Google's Gemini image tool, nicknamed Nano Banana, to edit or build a photo. The model is Gemini 2.5 Flash Image. You give it a picture plus a short instruction saying what to make and what to keep, and it returns the edited image. Banana is the nickname, not part of the wording.

faqs.q: Which banana prompt is the most popular?
faqs.a: The action-figure one, where you become a boxed collectible toy with plastic shine and fake packaging, traveled the furthest. The storefront prompt and the retro film-era swap were close behind. They spread because they keep your face recognizable while changing everything else, so the same wording works for anyone who pastes it in.

faqs.q: Should I use Nano Banana or Nano Banana Pro?
faqs.a: Use the standard Gemini 2.5 Flash Image for quick face-keeping edits, it is fast and free in the app. Switch to Nano Banana Pro, which came with Gemini 3, when your prompt needs readable text in the image like a sign or a label, or when you want stronger reasoning about what you asked for.

faqs.q: Where do I run a banana prompt for free?
faqs.a: The Gemini app has a free tier that covers most casual edits. Open it, upload one clear photo, paste the prompt, and run it. Heavy or batch use can hit limits or move you to the paid API at a few cents per image. Try a prompt free first and only pay if you generate in bulk.

faqs.q: Why is my banana prompt not keeping my face?
faqs.a: The style words are usually overpowering the likeness. Move keep my exact face and skin tone to the start of the prompt and ease off the heavy look language. Start from a sharp, well-lit photo since a blurry input always drifts. Run it two or three more times and pick the closest result.
